If some other vowel in a dictionary entry is accented, the dictionary shows an accent mark (´) over that vowel. The most common use of accents is in words with the special ending ve, meaning 'the place that'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final vowel of the citation/dictionary form (noun, or verb stem without its =k/=m and other endings), i.e. on the root/stem-final syllable; prefixes precede it and all suffixal endings (switch-reference/tense =k, =m, -pch, nominalizer -ve, etc.) are unstressed and never attract or shift the stress. Lexical exceptions with non-final stress in the dictionary form are marked with a written accent. In surface words this yields root stress rather than a fixed edge position (final in unsuffixed citation forms, penultimate or earlier once endings are added).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Dictionary says nothing. Crawford 1976 (same directory) reports secondary stress on certain verbal suffixes containing /u/ (-um, -tum, -sum, -kum) and on the reduced 'say' suffix -e, which she attributes to their origin in reduced verb roots (idu: 'be', i'i: 'say').
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose dictionary form is not final-stressed carry a written accent mark; all -ve 'the place that' nominalizations are stressed on the vowel before -ve; p.11: 'In most Mojave words listed in the Dictionary, the last vowel is accented.' Kroeber 1911 (pp.63-65) heard many words as final-accented but others (ka'veik 'south', pa'ya 'all', vi'ka 'seven', a'ha 'water' vs ah'a' 'cottonwood', a've 'rattlesnake' vs ave' 'mouse') as non-final or evenly balanced, and argued the accent is realized mainly as raised pitch (about a major third) rather than intensity.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is framed on the dictionary citation form (word without inflectional endings); explicitly says added endings do not receive or move the accent, so the domain is the stem/root within the morphological word. Pedagogical register (pronunciation guide for learners) but authored by the principal modern describer of Mojave (Munro). Based primarily on one speaker (Nellie Brown), Colorado River Indian Reservation, Parker AZ.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Mojave as spoken on the Colorado River Indian Reservation near Parker, Arizona (primarily one speaker, Nellie Brown); same language as Glottolog moha1256 'Mohave' (ISO mov); no dialect split is recognized in Glottolog. Kroeber 1911 recorded Mohave speakers at Needles/Fort Mojave area.

new_statements.quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. [p. 239] ... When both the root and pre-root syllable have short vowels, or when the pre-root vowel is long and the root vowel short, stress is perceived on the pre-root vowel (types a and b). When the pre-root vowel is short and the root vowel long, stress is perceived on the root (types c1, 2, and 3) ... We can therefore assume that Mojave, like other Yuman languages, has underlying stress on the root and derives the surface stress patterns by the application of stress retraction rules embodying the generalizations just stated. [p. 249]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Munro, Brown & Crawford 1992 statement (accent normally on the last vowel of the dictionary form, i.e. the root, unchanged when endings are added; non-final accents marked). Langdon gives the same underlying placement (stress is morphological, on the root, hence normally the last syllable of the uninflected word) and adds what the catalog lacks: the vowel-length-conditioned surface retraction to the pre-root syllable, the pitch correlate, the restoration of root stress in connected speech, the three lexical exceptions and the instrumental confirmation. It also supplies a citable statement that the catalog's empty 'rule' field can be filled with: morphological ro…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Underlying word stress is morphological: it sits on the (typically monosyllabic) root, which because Yuman words are built mostly with prefixes is normally the last syllable of an uninflected word; suffixes/enclitics never attract stress and other syllables are never perceived as stressed. Mojave alone among Yuman languages shows surface stress shifts, and Langdon shows these are predictable from vowel length in the pre-root and root syllables: short+short or long+short -> stress perceived on the pre-root syllable (e.g. ?aha 'water', ?a:hma 'quail'); short+long -> stress on the root (?aspa: 'eagle', ?avi: 'rock'), with an optional pre-root variant when the long root vowel is followed by a voiceless consonant (hupa:ka ~ hupa:ka 'snow'); long+long -> either syllable or both perceived as stressed (?i:pa: 'man'). Perceived stress coincides with the highest pitch (p. 250, confirming Kroeber 1911), and in connected discourse all forms surface with root stress (p. 252: ?ata:yk 'a lot', ?ata:yta:hank 'a whole lot'). The 1977 Epilogue (pp. 252-253) reports UCSD instrumental traces: a vowel with both highest F0 and highest amplitude is invariably heard as stressed; pitch alone, amplitude alone or length alone can also be heard as stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: For Mojave specifically nothing beyond the type-d observation that with two long vowels 'both are perceived as equally stressed' (p. 249). For Yuman generally (Diegueno examples, p. 240): the only reduction of a stressed syllable is to secondary stress on the first member of a compound, 'thus maintaining the preference for primary stress on the last syllable', and this secondary stress may reduce further to become indistinguishable from unstressed material. Footnote 4 (p. 257) notes that some investigators (Redden 1966, Halpern 1946-47) describe Yuman suffixes with primary stress, which Langdon treats as separate words.
new_statements.exceptions: Three apparent exceptions to the length-based generalizations (p. 252, ex. 21): ?a?i: 'wood', ?kari: 'basket', ?amma:t 'ground', all with a short pre-root vowel and a long root vowel but stress perceived on the first syllable; Langdon suggests the two glottal stops in 'wood' let stress be heard on the first syllable, and that 'basket' (which Munro hears with a short root vowel) and 'ground' (short root vowel by comparative evidence) really belong to pattern a. Kroeber's (1911) minimal pairs ?aha 'water' / ?ah?a: 'cottonwood', ?a:ve 'rattlesnake' / ?ave: 'mouse', ?i:do 'my eye' / ?i:do: 'willow' are cited (p. 248) as the stress-placement contrasts that the length analysis explains. Footnote 14 (p. 258): 'willow' placed under pattern d1 on comparative evidence despite tape versions with a final short vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: Langdon's Mojave data are from tapes of two Mojave speakers, Thomas Stevens and Nellie Brown, recorded by Pamela Munro and Linda Munsen, transcribed independently by Langdon and Donald Crook and checked against Munro's field notes (p. 248, fn. 13); Nellie Brown is also co-author of the 1992 dictionary, so the two statements rest on the same speaker community (Colorado River Mojave, River Yuman). No dialect is distinguished. Langdon's article also treats Diegueno, Kiliwa, Cocopa, Paipai and Yavapai; only pp. 239-241 (general Yuman) and pp. 248-256 concern Mojave.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the sources on the underlying placement: Langdon 1977 (opened) and the catalog's existing Munro, Brown & Crawford 1992 statement both put Mojave word stress on the root, which is the last syllable of the uninflected word, with affixes never taking it. The one thing a reader should not miss is the surface picture: Langdon documents (pp. 248-252) that Mojave, uniquely in Yuman, is often perceived with stress on the pre-root syllable, that the place of perceived stress is predictable from the short/long pattern of the pre-root and root vowels, and that the main cue is pitch; Kroeber 1911 (pp. 63-65, already held by the project from the our reading, not in this works list) had reported the same variable non-final accents and concluded that 'heightened pitch rather than increased stress constitutes the normal accent in Mohave'. Langdon reconciles Kroeber's observations with root stress by treating the non-final cases as surface retraction, restored in connected discourse. Munro 1992's 'normally comes on the last vowel.. If some other vowel.. is accented, the dictionary shows an accent mark' is the same picture stated as a lexicographic convention. Munro 1976 could not be opened.

sources.note: The Mojave Alphabet (p.11): in most words the last vowel is accented; an accent mark is written over accented non-final vowels. Pronunciation Notes (pp.316-317): main accent/stress normally on the last vowel (last syllable) of the word as listed in the dictionary; endings such as -ve 'the place that' and other verb endings are never accented; the accent stays on the last vowel of the dictionary form and does not move when endings are added. Intro (p.4) also notes a short/long vowel contrast in both stressed and unstressed positions.
